english: I'll message you later.
tip: -(으)ㄹ게요 = I'll (a promise to the listener): 카톡할게요 (katokhalgeyo).

english: I use stickers a lot.
tip: 쓰다 (sseuda) means both 'use' and 'write': 이모티콘을 써요 (imotikoneul sseoyo) = I use stickers. The same verb also writes letters and texts.

english: Could you give me your phone number?
tip: 좀 (jom) softens requests: 좀 알려 주세요 (jom allyeo juseyo) = please let me know.

target: 회의 중에는 휴대폰을 무음으로 해 놓아요.
english: I keep my phone on silent in meetings.
tip: -아/어 놓다 (-a/eo nota) marks a state you set and leave in place: 무음으로 해 놓아요 (mueumeuro hae noayo) = set it to silent and keep it that way.

english: I used up all my data.
tip: 다 (da) before a verb means completely: 데이터를 다 썼어요 (deitareul da sseosseoyo) = used up all the data. Works anywhere – 다 먹었어요 (da meogeosseoyo) = ate it all.

english: The battery's dead.
tip: 다 됐어요 (da dwaesseoyo), literally 'has all become', is the everyday 'it died / ran out': 배터리가 다 됐어요 (baeteoriga da dwaesseoyo). Works for parking time too.

english: Could you lend me a charger?
tip: V-어 주세요 = please (do for me): 빌려 주세요 (billyeo juseyo) = please lend me.

english: I left my charger at home.
tip: English 'left it at home' is two verbs in Korean: 놓고 왔어요 (noko wasseoyo) = put it down and came. You say both the placing – 놓다 (nota) – and the coming – 오다 (oda).

english: My phone is charging.
tip: -고 있어요 = is ...ing: 충전하고 있어요 (chungjeonhago isseoyo) = is charging.

english: Where can I charge?
tip: -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 = can: 충전할 수 있어요? (chungjeonhal su isseoyo?) = can I charge?

english: Give this app a try.
tip: V-어 보세요 = try ...ing: 써 보세요 (sseo boseyo) = try it out.

english: I couldn't log into the app.
tip: 못 (mot) = can't, blocked or unable – different from 안 (an) = simply don't: 로그인을 못 했어요 (rogeineul mot haesseoyo) means the login failed, not that you skipped it.

english: Shall we take a selfie here?
tip: 찍을까요? (jjigeulkkayo?) – the -(으)ㄹ까요 ending means 'shall we?'. Korean has no separate word for 'shall'; the whole suggestion lives in the verb ending.

english: My phone suddenly shut off.
tip: 꺼지다 (kkeojida) = turn off by itself; 끄다 (kkeuda) = turn it off. 갑자기 꺼졌어요 (gapjagi kkeojyeosseoyo) blames the phone – nobody switched it off.

english: There's no sound.
tip: Sound comes out on its own in Korean – 소리가 나다 (soriga nada = sound emerges). So 'no sound' is 소리가 안 나요 (soriga an nayo): the sound isn't coming out.

english: The repair fee was way too much.
tip: -비 (-bi) tacks 'fee' onto almost anything: 수리비가 (suribiga) = the repair cost, 택시비 (taeksibi) = taxi fare, 교통비 (gyotongbi) = transport costs.

english: Press and hold the power button.
tip: -게 (-ge) turns an adjective into a how-word: 길다 (gilda = long) becomes 길게 눌러 주세요 (gilge nulleo juseyo) = press long, i.e. long-press.

english: Just tap here.
tip: -(으)면 돼요 = just do X: 누르면 돼요 (nureumyeon dwaeyo) = pressing works.

english: The clothes I ordered haven't arrived.
tip: V-ㄴ + noun = that I ...ed: 주문한 옷 (jumunhan ot) = the clothes I ordered.

english: It didn't fit, so I got a refund.
tip: -아서 = so: 안 맞아서 환불했어요 (an majaseo hwanbulhaesseoyo).

english: I bought shoes during the sale.
tip: 때 (ttae) after a noun means 'at the time of': 세일 때 (seil ttae) = during the sale. No preposition needed – the noun plus 때 (ttae) does it all.

english: Grandma loves video calls.
tip: When the subject is someone honored, the verb takes -세요 (-seyo): 할머니는 좋아하세요 (halmeonineun joahaseyo) – grandma's verb gets the respect, not her name.

english: I bought a new laptop.
tip: 노트북 (noteubuk) looks like 'notebook' but means laptop – Konglish: 노트북을 샀어요 (noteubugeul sasseoyo) = bought a laptop. A paper notebook is 공책 (gongchaek).

english: My work computer won't turn on today.
tip: 켜지다 (kyeojida) = turn on by itself, the flip side of 켜다 (kyeoda = turn it on): 안 켜져요 (an kyeojyeoyo) = it won't come on, no matter who's pressing.

english: Don't look at your phone while driving.
tip: -지 마세요 = please don't: 보지 마세요 (boji maseyo) = don't look.

english: I put my phone down when I eat.
tip: -(으)ㄹ 때 = when: 먹을 때 (meogeul ttae) = when eating.

english: I can't live without the internet.
tip: 없이 못 살아요 (eopsi mot sarayo) = can't live without it.

english: Seollal is the lunar New Year.
tip: 설날 (seollal) follows the lunar calendar – 음력 (eumnyeok) – so it lands in late January or February, never on January 1.

target: 떡국을 먹으면 한 살 더 먹어요.
english: When you eat tteokguk, you turn a year older.
tip: Koreans eat their age: 나이를 먹다 (naireul meokda) = get older, literally 'eat age'. 한 살 더 먹어요 (han sal deo meogeoyo) = eat one more year.

target: 그래서 설날에 나이를 한 살 먹어요.
english: So on Seollal everyone gains a year of age.
tip: Koreans eat their age: 나이를 한 살 먹어요 (nai-reul han sal meogeoyo) is literally 'eat one year of age'. 먹다 (meokda = eat) is the normal way to say you get a year older.
